name: iced (iced-x86)
baseline: Capstone (decode+format throughput); Zydis and Intel XED also measured in the same harness
workload: Decoding (and decoding plus formatting) the code section of a 64-bit x86 binary repeatedly in the disas-bench harness, reported as MB/s of machine code.
claimed_speedup: disas-bench charts (approximate readings): on the Ryzen 9 9950X iced decode+format is about 160 MB/s versus Capstone about 28, Zydis (full) about 34 and XED about 21 MB/s; iced decode-only is about 362 MB/s versus Zydis (full) about 50 and XED about 67 MB/s. On the i9-13900K iced decode+format is about 166 MB/s versus Capstone about 26 and Zydis about 35 MB/s; decode-only about 391 MB/s. Ratio to Capstone on decode+format about 5.7x (AMD) and 6.4x (Intel) (derived from page data, chart readings). README claim: 'Decodes >250 MB/s and decode+format >130 MB/s'.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.88.0 (AMD run) / 1.90.0 (Intel run); bench crate profile.release opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1; Capstone baseline built by cc -O3 with GCC 13.3 / 14.2 (bench/*/Cargo.toml, bench/cs/Makefile)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8.0) and Intel Core i9-13900K (Debian trixie, Linux 6.12.48)
tradeoffs: Rust crate; first-party bindings listed in the README for .NET, Java, Python, JavaScript (WebAssembly) and Lua, but no C/C++ API is named, so use from C++ needs a wrapper. Also contains an encoder and code assembler (no speed claim for those). The harness enables the 'fast_fmt' formatter feature.
caveats: The README's own '>250 MB/s' figure links to the same disas-bench harness. yaxpeax-x86 decodes faster than iced in decode-only rows. Chart values are visual readings of bar-chart PNGs (approximate, roughly +/-3 MB/s), not a text table. Capstone appears only as a decode+format row, so decode+format rows are the like-for-like comparison; formatted output differs in detail between libraries. The input binary and the harness's disassembly mode details were not examined. Baseline Capstone was not benchmarked against libopcodes/objdump here.

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper (PDF opened): the Montgomery multiplication kernel from OpenSSL's big-number library is 16 lines shorter and 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 output and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly; across the benchmark kernels STOKE matches gcc -O3 and icc -O3 starting from llvm -O0 and in several cases exceeds both. ASPLOS 2017 paper (PDF opened): 'median and average speedup of 25% over the libraries shipped by Google' for 13 libc string functions with formal verification. README tutorial: popcount drops from about 1.05 s to about 0.13 s versus a g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline build.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: Speedups are on hand-picked small kernels, and the ASPLOS 2013 Figure 11 reports speedup over llvm -O0 with STOKE 'comparable' to gcc -O3 and icc -O3 on many kernels, not always faster. The 2017 baseline is Google's shipped NaCl libc code (already constrained by SFI alignment rules), not a plain gcc -O3 build. A 2022 TU Delft bachelor thesis, seen only as a WebSearch snippet (not opened), reports that STOKE often fails to match gcc -O3 and struggles with loops. Not a benchmark of assemble time. Same repo holds both papers (docs/papers/asplos13.pdf, asplos17.pdf, cacm16.pdf and others).
found_via: WebSearch 'superoptimizer outperforms gcc -O3 assembly speedup github open source (STOKE OR Souper OR Minotaur)'; then github.com/StanfordPL/stoke README and docs/papers PDFs fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com and pdftotext

name: Minotaur
baseline: LLVM -O3 (clang) output quality, i.e. LLVM's own peephole and vectorization passes
workload: Runtime of code compiled with and without the Minotaur LLVM pass: SPEC CPU 2017, the GMP benchmark suite and LibYUV.
claimed_speedup: OOPSLA 2024 paper, per WebSearch result text only (paper not opened): SPEC CPU 2017 mean speedup 1.5% on Intel (1.2% on AMD) with a maximum of 4.5% on 638.imagick; GMP benchmark suite mean 7.3% with a maximum of 13% on an Intel Cascade Lake processor; LibYUV geomean 1.029x on AMD Zen 3.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (GMP), AMD Zen 3 (LibYUV); other CPUs per paper not confirmed
tradeoffs: Runs as an LLVM opt pass or via minotaur-cc / minotaur-c++ wrappers; needs a patched, RTTI- and EH-enabled LLVM build, Alive2, Z3 and Redis (offline cache mode), which makes the build heavy. Synthesis time adds to compile time.
caveats: All numbers come from search-result text of the paper (arxiv 2306.00229, blocked in this environment) and have not been checked on the paper itself; the repo README has no performance numbers and no evaluation directory was seen. Gains on SPEC are small (1.2-1.5% mean). Peer review (OOPSLA 2024) taken from a SPLASH 2024 programme page snippet. It is an LLVM IR superoptimizer, so only loosely 'assembly tooling'.
found_via: WebSearch 'superoptimizer outperforms gcc -O3 ...' and 'Minotaur SIMD-oriented superoptimizer LLVM evaluation speedup SPEC CPU 2017 geomean results'; opened github.com/minotaur-toolkit/minotaur

name: Unison
baseline: LLVM's register allocator and instruction scheduler (output quality, Hexagon, ARM and MIPS back ends)
workload: Estimated speedup and code size of functions from MediaBench and SPEC CPU2006 compiled with Unison's integrated combinatorial register allocation and instruction scheduling versus LLVM.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of the arXiv/TOPLAS paper only (paper not opened): mean estimated speedup ranges from 1.1% to 10% and mean code size reduction from 1.3% to 3.8% depending on the architecture; the authors say execution on Hexagon confirms that the estimated speedup becomes actual speedup.
hardware: Hexagon (execution check); estimates for ARM and MIPS
tradeoffs: Haskell tool driving constraint solvers, used through a Unison-enabled LLVM fork (github.com/unison-code/llvm); solving time is far higher than LLVM's heuristics; targets Hexagon, ARM and MIPS rather than x86.
caveats: Numbers are 'estimated' speedups from a static cost model, not measured runtimes, except for the Hexagon confirmation. The repo README has no performance claims or links to results, and the paper and project site were not reachable here, so all numbers are from search-result text. Peer review (ACM TOPLAS 2019 journal version) inferred from a doi 10.1145/3332373 snippet. Last commit is 2023.
found_via: WebSearch 'Unison combinatorial register allocation instruction scheduling LLVM speedup github paper OR GreenThumb superoptimizer open source'; opened github.com/unison-code/unison

name: SuperCoder
workload: Runtime speedup of LLM-rewritten x86 assembly versus the gcc -O3 assembly on a benchmark of 8,072 real-world programs averaging 130 lines (CodeNet-derived), with test-based correctness checks.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of arXiv 2505.11480 only (paper not opened): the RL-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model reaches a 95.0% test pass rate and a 1.46x average speedup over gcc -O3; the strongest baseline LLM (Claude-opus-4) reaches 51.5% pass rate and 1.43x average speedup.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 baseline stated in search-result text; flags and timing harness (hyperfine) not stated in the README
tradeoffs: Probabilistic output: correctness is test-based (95.0% pass rate, not formal equivalence), so rewrites need independent verification. Needs a GPU-capable RL setup (verl) to retrain; model weights and dataset are listed on Hugging Face in the README.
caveats: Numbers come from search-result text only; the repo README has no results section and states no hardware or compiler flags. Averages are over test-passing programs as reported by the authors, so failed rewrites are excluded from the speedup mean (not verified on the paper). Preprint status; 2 commits in the repo.
found_via: WebSearch 'SuperCoder assembly superoptimization large language models reinforcement learning speedup over gcc -O3 github repository'; opened github.com/Anjiang-Wei/SuperCoder and its README

name: SLOTHY
baseline: unscheduled 'clean' hand-written assembly and prior hand-optimized implementations of the same kernels (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs, FFT, X25519); no compiler baseline stated on the pages opened
workload: Instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining of hand-written Arm AArch64, Armv8.1-M and RISC-V assembly for cryptographic and DSP kernels.
claimed_speedup: README: SLOTHY has been used 'to provide the fastest known implementations of various cryptographic and DSP primitives' (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs for Cortex-A55/A72/M55/M85, FFT for Cortex-M55/M85, X25519 for Cortex-A55); no speedup numbers on any page opened. Related adoption number: the AWS-LC pull request that imported the s2n-bignum X25519 rewrite (partly SLOTHY-generated) reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup') on Graviton 2, but that gain is not attributable to SLOTHY alone.
hardware: Targets Cortex-M55, M85, A55 (supported), A72, Cortex-X/Neoverse-V, Apple M1 (experimental) and XuanTie C908
stars_or_usage: 352 stars; adopted in AWS-LC / s2n-bignum, Arm EndpointAI CMSIS DSP and mlkem-native
tradeoffs: Microarchitecture-specific by design: each output is scheduled for one core model (portability note: code tuned for Cortex-A55 is not tuned for other cores). Solver time is seconds to minutes for under 50 instructions and minutes to hours for up to 150 instructions; larger kernels need heuristics. Python tool using Google OR-Tools.
caveats: The paper (CHES 2024, eprint 2022/1303) and its numbers could not be opened (eprint.iacr.org blocked), so no measured speedup is confirmed. The repo ships the clean and optimized sources and a reproduction artifact (paper/, paper/artifact) but cycle benchmarks need physical boards and were not run or read. The AWS-LC PR (#1469) was closed unmerged and mixes an algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling.
found_via: github.com/topics/superoptimization (WebFetch); opened the slothy README, paper/README.md, LICENSE and AWS-LC / s2n-bignum PR pages

name: Asmc
baseline: MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler 6.15 and 10.0), also compared with JWasm and UASM
workload: Assemble time of a 21,000-line MASM-syntax source in a forum user's test.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 1200 ms for Asmc versus 1800 ms for MASM 6.15 and 10.0 (1.5x, derived from snippet data), 1480 ms JWasm, 1630 ms UAsm64; a different poster in the same snippet puts Asmc 'about 25-30% faster than UAsm'. The README itself makes no speed claim.
tradeoffs: Written in assembly (MASM syntax, self-hosted); runs on Windows and Linux; GPL licence; MASM compatibility is not perfect (the project adds its own macro/language extensions and claims MASM v14 AVX-512 support while its Version macro is v10).
caveats: The MASM-compatible assembler timing numbers appear only in a WebSearch result snippet of a masm32.com forum thread (page unreachable here: ENOTFOUND), recorded as 'snippet only'; the same thread says on a 21,000-line source MASM 6.15 and 10.0 took 1800 ms each, UAsm64 1630 ms, JWasm 1480 ms and AsmC 1200 ms. Anecdotal forum measurement, no hardware, flags or versions seen. One poster in the same snippet says the same extensions make him distrust the tool, and another snippet claim of a '7-8x' speed-up over MASM contradicts the 1.5x timing above.
found_via: WebSearch 'MASM compatible assembler faster than MASM assembly speed UASM JWasm Asmc github'; opened github.com/nidud/asmc README, license.txt and commits page
